lead: Every circuit in this unit comes from one rule: with negative feedback, the op-amp drives its output until the two inputs sit at the same voltage. After this unit you can design amplifiers, summers, instrumentation amplifiers, integrators, current converters, log amps, precision rectifiers and Schmitt triggers, and compute each output from its resistor and capacitor values.
about: The unit turns the op-amp from a component into a design tool. Chapter 6.1 fixes the ideal model and the virtual ground rule; 6.2 uses that rule for the inverting, non-inverting and follower circuits; 6.3 adds inputs to get summers and subtractors; 6.4 chains three op-amps into an instrumentation amplifier. 6.5 swaps resistors for capacitors to integrate and differentiate, and 6.6 makes the output a current instead of a voltage. 6.7 exploits the exponential diode law for log, antilog and multiplication. 6.8 puts a diode inside the feedback loop for precision rectifiers, peak detectors and sample-and-hold. 6.9 removes the feedback to get a comparator, then adds positive feedback for the Schmitt trigger and window detector.

chapters.idea: An ideal op-amp has infinite gain, so with negative feedback it forces v₊ = v₋ (a virtual short) and its inputs draw no current.
chapters.depth: Ideal properties: infinite open-loop gain A_OL, infinite input resistance, zero output resistance, infinite bandwidth, zero offset and drift. Draw the ideal model as a controlled source A_OL·v_d with R_in across the inputs and R_o in series with the output; some syllabi call this the IOA model. Open-loop characteristic: plot v_out against v_d and mark the linear strip and saturation at about 1 V inside the supply rails. The linear strip is only 2V_sat/A_OL wide, tens of microvolts. Virtual short and virtual ground, and the exact condition for them: negative feedback and the output inside the linear range. One table of ideal against practical values (A_OL ≈ 10⁵, R_in = 1 MΩ to 10¹² Ω, R_o = 50–100 Ω, offset in mV, bias current in nA to pA).

figure.title: Ideal op-amp model
figure.aria: The ideal op-amp model: the two inputs produce v_d, a controlled source multiplies it by A_OL, and a small output resistance feeds v_out.

chapters.example: An op-amp has A_OL = 2 × 10⁵ and ±12 V supplies. Find the output for v_d = 100 µV, and the largest v_d that keeps the amplifier in its linear region. Ideal output = 2 × 10⁵ × 100 × 10⁻⁶ = 20 V. The supplies allow only about ±11 V, so the output saturates at +11 V. For saturation, v_d = 11 / (2 × 10⁵) = 55 µV. Any differential input larger than 55 µV therefore drives this op-amp into saturation when it is used open loop.
chapters.trap: Writing v₊ = v₋ for an open-loop or positive-feedback circuit. The virtual short exists only while negative feedback holds the output inside the linear range.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 (differential pair, common-mode gain, CMRR, offset, slew rate); Unit 4 (negative feedback and loop gain).
chapters.leave: Internal stages, frequency compensation and full parameter definitions to Unit 5; gain–bandwidth product and high-frequency roll-off to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Two resistors around the virtual ground set a gain of −R_f/R₁ (inverting) or 1 + R_f/R₁ (non-inverting), and the follower is the non-inverting case with R₁ open.
chapters.depth: Inverting amplifier: v_out = −(R_f/R₁)v_in, input resistance is exactly R₁, the inverting node is a virtual ground. Non-inverting amplifier: v_out = (1 + R_f/R₁)v_in, input resistance set by the op-amp itself, so it is very high. Voltage follower (also called a buffer or unity-gain amplifier): gain 1, used for impedance transformation, driving a load from a sensor, and isolating a divider. Design steps for a target gain, then guidelines for resistor choice: keep R_f below about 1 MΩ, keep R₁ above about 1 kΩ, add a bias-current compensating resistor on the other input, and cascade two stages by multiplying gains. Short section on finite A_OL (gain error ≈ (1 + R_f/R₁)/A_OL), finite input resistance and non-zero output resistance, because some syllabi ask for it. Parasitic capacitance at the inverting node causes peaking: name it, do not analyse it.

figure.title: Inverting amplifier signal path
figure.aria: Signal path of the inverting amplifier: R₁ drops v_in across a virtual ground, and R_f carries the same current back from the output.

chapters.example: An inverting amplifier uses R₁ = 10 kΩ and R_f = 100 kΩ with v_in = 0.2 V. Find the gain, the output and the input current, then repeat for the non-inverting connection with the same resistors. Gain = −100k/10k = −10, so v_out = −2 V; the input current is 0.2 V / 10 kΩ = 20 µA and the same 20 µA flows in R_f. Non-inverting: gain = 1 + 100k/10k = 11, so v_out = +2.2 V. With A_OL = 10⁵ the inverting gain is actually −10/(1 + 11/10⁵) = −9.999, an error of about 0.01 %.
chapters.trap: Using R_f/R₁ for the non-inverting gain, or believing the inverting input is a high-resistance node — it is R₁ to ground through the source.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1 (ideal model, virtual ground); Unit 4 (negative feedback).
chapters.leave: Offset and bias-current error analysis to 6.1's model plus the parameter values from Unit 5; frequency response of the closed loop to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Many inputs through their own resistors share one virtual ground, so their currents add; a subtractor is a difference amplifier that removes a common voltage when its resistor ratios match.
chapters.depth: Inverting summer (weighted summer): v_out = −R_f(v₁/R₁ + v₂/R₂ + …). Equal resistors give the average, scaled by −R_f/R. Scaling inputs by binary weights turns it into a simple DAC, which links forward to Unit 7. Non-inverting summer: use superposition with the divider at the non-inverting input and the gain 1 + R_f/R₁; say briefly why most designers prefer the inverting version (true virtual ground, no common-mode voltage at the inputs). Subtractor (difference amplifier) with four resistors: v_out = (R_f/R₁)(v₂ − v₁) when R₃/R₂ = R_f/R₁; derive it once by superposition. Effect of resistor tolerance: the common-mode gain is no longer zero, and with 1 % resistors the worst-case CMRR falls to about 25, that is roughly 28 dB, because CMRR ≈ 1/(4t) for a fractional tolerance t. Applications: audio mixing, level shifting, bridge difference, sensor offset removal.

figure.title: Three-input inverting summer
figure.aria: Three input voltages become currents through R₁, R₂ and R₃, add at the virtual ground, and the total flows through R_f to the output.

chapters.example: An inverting summer has R_f = 10 kΩ with v₁ = 1 V through R₁ = 10 kΩ, v₂ = 0.5 V through R₂ = 20 kΩ, and v₃ = 0.2 V through R₃ = 4 kΩ. Find v_out. Currents are 100 µA, 25 µA and 50 µA, total 175 µA. v_out = −175 µA × 10 kΩ = −1.75 V. Next, a subtractor has R₁ = R₂ = R₃ = R_f = 10 kΩ, v₁ = 2 V at the inverting input and v₂ = 1.5 V at the non-inverting input; then v_out = v₂ − v₁ = −0.5 V.
chapters.trap: Assuming a difference amplifier rejects common-mode perfectly. It rejects only as well as its four resistors match; 1 % parts wreck the CMRR.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 6.1 and 6.2 (virtual ground, inverting and non-inverting gains); superposition from basic circuit theory.
chapters.leave: Full DAC design (R-2R ladder, weighted resistor) to Unit 7; op-amp internal CMRR to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Two buffered inputs and one difference amplifier give a gain of (1 + 2R/R_G)(R_f/R₁) with gigaohm input resistance and very high CMRR.
chapters.depth: Three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier: input stage of two non-inverting buffers sharing R_G, so the differential gain is 1 + 2R/R_G while the common-mode gain of that stage is 1; second stage is a difference amplifier with gain R_f/R₁; total gain is the product. Show why the single difference amplifier fails here: low input resistance loads the bridge and its CMRR depends on resistor matching. Two-op-amp version and its drawback (unequal input resistance on the two inputs) in three lines. Monolithic parts give CMRR above 100 dB and gain error set by R_G tolerance. Applications: strain-gauge bridge, ECG and EEG front ends, thermocouple, motor current sensing through a shunt. Practical one-liners: keep leads short, use a driven shield for the ECG case.

figure.title: Three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier
figure.aria: The instrumentation amplifier: two buffers give high input impedance and a first-stage gain fixed by R_G, and a difference amplifier removes the common-mode voltage.

chapters.example: An instrumentation amplifier uses R = 25 kΩ in both input-stage feedback paths, R_G = 1 kΩ, and a second stage with all four resistors 10 kΩ. Find the total gain and the output for a 5 mV differential input riding on a 2 V common-mode voltage. First stage gain = 1 + 2(25k)/1k = 51; second stage gain = 1; total 51. Output for the differential part = 51 × 5 mV = 255 mV. Common-mode gain = 51/10⁵ = 5.1 × 10⁻⁴ for CMRR = 100 dB, so 2 V of common mode adds only 2 V × 5.1 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 1 mV at the output.
chapters.trap: Writing the first-stage gain as 1 + R/R_G and forgetting the factor 2, or blaming R_G for CMRR when CMRR is set by the difference-amplifier resistors.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 6.1–6.3 (non-inverting gain, difference amplifier, resistor matching).
chapters.leave: Op-amp CMRR origin to Unit 5; bridge and transducer physics to the measurement course; active filters on the same front end to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: Replacing a resistor with a capacitor makes the output proportional to the integral of the input, and swapping R and C makes it proportional to the derivative.
chapters.depth: Integrator: v_out = −(1/R₁C)∫v_in dt over the interval, time constant R₁C, step input gives a ramp of slope −v_in/(R₁C), square wave in gives triangle out. Frequency response falls at 20 dB per decade above 1/(2πR₁C). Practical integrator: R_f in parallel with C limits the DC gain to −R_f/R₁ and stops drift to saturation; add the bias-current resistor on the other input. Differentiator: v_out = −R C dv_in/dt, triangle in gives square out, gain rises with frequency so noise dominates; add R₁ in series with C to cap the high-frequency gain at −R/R₁ and a small capacitor across R_f. Applications: PID controllers, analog computers, waveform shaping, edge detection, charge amplifiers. Name the units: R₁ in ohms, C in farads, R₁C in seconds.

figure.aria: Gain against frequency for a 100 µs integrator falling at 20 dB per decade and a differentiator rising at 20 dB per decade, both crossing 0 dB at 1.6 kHz.

chapters.example: An inverting integrator has R₁ = 10 kΩ and C = 0.01 µF. Find the output 1 ms after a 1 V step is applied. R₁C = 10⁴ × 10⁻⁸ = 10⁻⁴ s = 100 µs. The slope is −v_in/(R₁C) = −1/10⁻⁴ = −10 000 V/s, that is −10 V per ms. After 1 ms the output would be −10 V, so on ±12 V supplies a 1 V step saturates the circuit in about 1 ms. Differentiator with the same R and C: a triangle of slope 1000 V/s gives v_out = −RC × slope = −10⁻⁴ × 1000 = −0.1 V.
chapters.trap: Omitting R_f in a practical integrator, so offset voltage and bias current walk the output to a rail; and forgetting the ideal differentiator gain rises without limit and turns noise into oscillation.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.2 (inverting configuration, virtual ground); capacitor current–voltage relation from basic circuit theory.
chapters.leave: Active filter design with these blocks to Unit 7; op-amp slew rate and bandwidth limits to Unit 5 and Unit 3.

chapters.idea: The op-amp can hold a fixed voltage across R, so the current it forces into a load is v_in/R and does not depend on the load; the reverse circuit turns an input current into a voltage.
chapters.depth: Voltage-to-current converter, floating load: load and R sit in the feedback path and the current is v_in/R. Grounded-load Howland current pump: four resistors, output current v_in/R, needs matched resistors so that the load current stays constant. Compliance: the maximum load resistance before the op-amp saturates, R_L(max) = (V_sat − v_in)/I. Current-to-voltage converter (transimpedance amplifier): v_out = −I_in R_f, input resistance near zero so it does not slow a photodiode; add a capacitor across R_f for stability against the source capacitance. Applications: LED and laser diode drivers, 4–20 mA current loop transmitter, photodiode front end, DAC current output to voltage.

figure.title: Voltage-to-current converter
figure.aria: Voltage-to-current conversion: the op-amp keeps the voltage across R equal to v_in, so the current pushed into the load is v_in divided by R.

chapters.example: A Howland current pump uses R = 1 kΩ and v_in = 2 V to drive a 500 Ω load from ±12 V supplies. Find the load current, the load voltage and the largest load allowed. I = 2 V / 1 kΩ = 2 mA, independent of the load. Load voltage = 2 mA × 500 Ω = 1 V. The op-amp output must reach 1 V + 2 V = 3 V, which is inside the rails. At the limit, output = 12 V gives R_L(max) = (12 − 2)/2 mA = 5 kΩ. For the reverse circuit, a photodiode delivers 10 µA into R_f = 100 kΩ, so v_out = −10 µA × 100 kΩ = −1 V.
chapters.trap: Assuming the current stays constant for any load. Past the compliance limit the op-amp saturates and the current collapses, and an unmatched Howland pump lets the current depend on R_L.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1 (virtual short) and 6.2 (inverting configuration); Ohm's law and op-amp saturation from 6.1.
chapters.leave: 4–20 mA loop hardware and industrial sensors to a measurements course; photodiode physics to the physics or sensors course.

chapters.idea: A diode or transistor in the feedback loop gives an output proportional to the logarithm of the input, and log plus add plus antilog multiplies two signals.
chapters.depth: Log amplifier: diode or BJT in feedback, v_out = −V_T ln(v_in/(I_S R)); V_T ≈ 26 mV at 300 K, giving about 60 mV per decade of input; input must be positive, and the output is temperature dependent through both V_T and I_S. Matched-transistor version cancels I_S; a thermistor or a difference of two logs removes part of the drift. Antilog (exponential) amplifier: exponential element in the input path, output proportional to e^(v_in/V_T). Analog multiplier by the log–antilog chain: v_out = v₁v₂/k, with k a scaling voltage; division and squaring come from the same blocks by changing the summer. One line: the Gilbert cell (variable transconductance) multiplier is the version inside most ICs, and only a few universities teach its internal analysis. Applications: dB readout, RMS-to-DC conversion, companding in telephony, AGC, power measurement.

figure.title: Log–antilog multiplier
figure.aria: A multiplier built from logarithms: each input is log-amplified, the two logs are added, and an antilog stage turns the sum back into the product.

chapters.example: A diode log amplifier has R = 10 kΩ, I_S = 10⁻¹⁴ A and V_T = 26 mV. Find v_out for v_in = 1 V, then for 0.1 V, and the change per decade. At 1 V, I = 100 µA and v_out = −0.026 ln(100 × 10⁻⁶ / 10⁻¹⁴) = −0.026 ln(10¹⁰) = −0.026 × 23.03 = −0.60 V. At 0.1 V, I = 10 µA and v_out = −0.026 × 20.72 = −0.54 V. The difference is 0.06 V, that is 60 mV per decade. Feeding the two logs into a summer and then an antilog with k = 10 V gives, for v₁ = 2 V and v₂ = 3 V, v_out = 2 × 3 / 10 = 0.6 V.
chapters.trap: Dropping the minus sign and forgetting temperature: V_T and I_S both move with temperature, so an uncompensated log amp drifts by millivolts per degree.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.3 (summing amplifier); diode equation and BJT exponential law from Unit 1 and Unit 2.
chapters.leave: Gilbert cell internals and OTA-based multipliers to Unit 5; dB and RMS measurement theory to a measurements course.

chapters.idea: Placing a diode inside the feedback loop divides its 0.7 V drop by the open-loop gain, so millivolt signals rectify accurately; a capacitor then holds the peak or samples the wave.
chapters.depth: Why precision is needed: a silicon diode needs about 0.6–0.7 V, so a 10 mV signal produces no output at all. Inverting and non-inverting half-wave precision rectifiers; full-wave precision rectifier with two op-amps and two diodes, including the waveform at each node. Limit on frequency: finite open-loop gain and slew rate mean these circuits work from DC to a few kHz or tens of kHz, and the op-amp must recover quickly from saturation, so a fast op-amp is chosen. Peak detector: diode, hold capacitor, buffer, with droop from leakage and bias current, and a reset switch. Sample-and-hold (also called track-and-hold): analog switch, hold capacitor, buffer; define acquisition time, aperture time, droop rate and hold-mode feedthrough; explain why an ADC needs it in front. Applications: digital multimeter, peak-reading meter, AM demodulation, ADC front end.

figure.aria: A sine input with the half-wave and full-wave outputs of precision rectifiers drawn from the same input, each reaching the full input amplitude.

chapters.example: A sine of 10 mV peak is applied to a half-wave rectifier with R₁ = R_f = 10 kΩ, first with a plain silicon diode and then with the diode inside the op-amp loop. Plain diode: the diode needs about 0.7 V to conduct, so the output stays at 0 V and the circuit is useless. Precision version: the op-amp raises its output until the diode conducts, so the feedback loop closes and v_out = −10 mV on one half cycle and 0 V on the other. Peak detector next: 1 V peak held on C = 0.01 µF, with 1 nA of bias current leaking away, droop = I/C = 1 nA / 10 nF = 100 V/s = 0.1 V per ms.
chapters.trap: Using a precision rectifier at high frequency. Above a few kHz the op-amp slew rate and falling open-loop gain make the output distort, and the op-amp takes time to come out of saturation.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.2 (inverting gain, feedback loop) and 6.1 (open-loop gain makes the diode drop negligible); diode behaviour from Unit 1.
chapters.leave: ADC sampling theory and aliasing to Unit 7; analog switch internal circuits to a digital or VLSI course.

chapters.idea: Without feedback the op-amp is a comparator that outputs one of two rails; adding positive feedback gives two thresholds, and two comparators give a window.
chapters.depth: Comparator: open-loop op-amp, output saturates at about ±(V_sat), a few microvolts of input swing the output fully, so it converts an analog level to a logic level. Response time and slew rate set the speed; open-collector comparators need a pull-up resistor; never use an op-amp as a fast comparator without checking recovery from saturation. Zero-crossing detector. Schmitt trigger (also called a regenerative comparator): positive feedback through R₂ gives upper and lower thresholds; with reference at 0 V, β = R₁/(R₁ + R₂), UTP = +βV_sat, LTP = −βV_sat, hysteresis width 2βV_sat. Show how hysteresis cleans a noisy slowly varying input and stops multiple counting. Inverting and non-inverting versions, and the design step from a required hysteresis width. Window detector: two comparators with references V_L and V_U plus an AND gate or diode logic, output high only while V_L < v_in < V_U. Applications: flash ADC comparator, thermostat, over- and under-voltage trip, zero-crossing in a dimmer.

figure.title: Schmitt trigger with positive feedback
figure.aria: A Schmitt trigger: the comparator output saturates to a rail and the R₁–R₂ divider returns a fraction of it to the positive input, creating two switching thresholds.

chapters.example: An inverting Schmitt trigger runs on ±12 V supplies with V_sat = ±11 V, R₁ = 10 kΩ from the input source to the positive input, R₂ = 20 kΩ from the output to the positive input, and V_ref = 0 V. Find both thresholds and the hysteresis width. β = R₁/(R₁ + R₂) = 10/30 = 1/3. UTP = +βV_sat = +11/3 = +3.67 V; LTP = −3.67 V. Hysteresis width = 7.33 V, so any noise smaller than that cannot cause extra output transitions. A window detector on the same supplies uses V_L = 3 V and V_U = 5 V, so its output is high only while 3 V < v_in < 5 V.
chapters.trap: Using R₂/(R₁ + R₂) as the feedback fraction instead of R₁/(R₁ + R₂), and forgetting that a plain comparator has no hysteresis, so a slow noisy input makes the output chatter.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1 (open-loop transfer curve and saturation); Unit 4 (positive feedback and the idea of two stable states).
chapters.leave: Astable and monostable multivibrators built on the same comparator to Unit 7; logic gate families for the AND stage to a digital course.
